title: 10-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet
web_title: 6. 10-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet
book_title: Chapter 6: Following the Cash — 10-Year Financials & Earnings Quality

epigraph.quote: “Sustained negative cash flow could impact our growth and business.”
epigraph.author: Aluwind Architectural Ltd., Prospectus dated 20 March 2024, Risk Factor 17

web_blocks.html: A literal ten-year record is not public. The company listed in April 2024, so the audited trail is short: restated FY21 to FY23 and H1 FY24 figures in the prospectus, the FY24, FY25 and FY26 annual reports, and half-year results to September 2026 [3][4][1][5]. I use FY21 to FY26 plus H1 FY27; FY21 to FY24 are standalone and the later periods consolidated. FY23 operating cash flow was later restated from +₹1.53 Cr to +₹0.94 Cr [3][4]; the tables use the prospectus figure, and on the restated figure the FY23 gap to profit is -₹1.76 Cr instead of -₹1.17 Cr.

web_blocks.caption: Profit and loss, FY21 to H1 FY27, ₹ Cr (prospectus, annual reports, H1 FY27 filing)
web_blocks.takeaway: Revenue rose 6.5 times in five years. EPS is not comparable (n/c) before FY24 because of the 62:10 bonus in January 2024. H1 FY27 is consolidated (standalone margin 13.5%, PAT ₹6.69 Cr). Sources: [3][4][1][5].

web_blocks.html: Revenue compounded about 45% a year from FY21 and profit after tax grew from ₹0.77 Cr to ₹10.45 Cr. Operating margin rose from 6% in FY22 to 14% in FY24 and has stayed between 11% and 14% since. Per share the picture is flatter: PAT rose 38.5% from FY24 to FY26 but EPS only 1.7%, because the IPO added 66 lakh shares to a base of 1.82 Cr [4][1]. The count has been 2,48,47,420 since April 2024, with 90,000 options granted in January 2026 [1].

web_blocks.caption: Balance sheet and working capital, ₹ Cr (FY21 to FY24 'unbilled and other' is all other current assets)
rows: As % of revenue (Sep-26 on last twelve months)
web_blocks.takeaway: Working capital has been 39% to 54% of revenue since FY21, so the business was always capital-hungry. The jump to 64% and 66% is on top of that base. Sources: [3][4][1][5]; ratios are my arithmetic.

web_blocks.html: The balance sheet explains the cash gap. Between March 2024 and March 2026, inventory grew from ₹11.3 Cr to ₹57.6 Cr, receivables including retention from ₹20.4 Cr to ₹39.1 Cr, and trade payables from ₹13.8 Cr to ₹40.1 Cr, while borrowings rose from ₹12.5 Cr to ₹41.3 Cr [4][1]. Suppliers financed some of the build, but not all of it, and the rest was funded by the IPO and the banks. Equity jumped in FY25 because of the IPO and has been rebuilt by retained profit since.

web_blocks.caption: Cash flow, ₹ Cr (FY23 as in the prospectus; capex is purchase of fixed assets)
web_blocks.takeaway: Operating cash flow has been below profit in six of the seven periods shown and below zero in FY22 and again in FY24, FY25 and FY26. Sources: [3][4][1][5].

web_blocks.html: The gap between profit and cash is the heart of this chapter. From FY24 to FY26 profit was ₹26.1 Cr and operating cash flow was -₹37.5 Cr. Four items show in the notes. Inventory more than doubled to ₹57.6 Cr, with raw material up from ₹17.4 Cr to ₹30.6 Cr and stores and spares from ₹5.1 Cr to ₹13.8 Cr. Profit is booked as work progresses, so ₹32.8 Cr is unbilled. Customers hold ₹13.7 Cr as retention. Advances fell ₹3.7 Cr [1]. Unbilled work plus retention, ₹46.4 Cr, is 4.4 times FY26 profit: income booked, not collected.

web_blocks.caption: From operating profit to operating cash flow, ₹ Cr (consolidated)
web_blocks.takeaway: Inventory is the largest single drain in both years and the largest single release in H1 FY27, while receivables kept absorbing cash. Source: [1][5].

web_blocks.html: The gap was financed in two steps. FY25 used ₹27.0 Cr of net IPO money. FY26 used banks: borrowings went from ₹13.1 Cr to ₹41.3 Cr and reached ₹46.0 Cr at September 2026 [1][5]. Of ₹52.5 Cr of financing in FY25 and FY26, operations absorbed ₹35.2 Cr and investing ₹16.1 Cr, which includes ₹6.0 Cr of assets and ₹12.1 Cr placed in deposits under lien, gold and property [1]. Lines are ICICI and Kotak cash credit at 8.15%, a ₹10 Cr working-capital loan and ₹9.1 Cr of unsecured bank and NBFC loans at up to 13.5%, repayable on demand and backed by four family guarantors [1]. Interest rose from ₹1.20 Cr to ₹2.16 Cr and was ₹2.25 Cr in H1 FY27 alone. Operating profit covered interest 9.1 times in FY25, 6.8 in FY26 and 4.0 in H1 FY27 (my arithmetic).

Return on equity fell from 19.3% in FY25 to 16.1% in FY26. Split into margin times asset turn times leverage, FY25 was 7.44% × 1.28 × 2.03 and FY26 was 7.54% × 1.02 × 2.09 (my arithmetic). Margin held. Asset turn fell because assets outgrew revenue, which is the working capital again, and leverage looks flat only because IPO equity offset new debt. The company's ROCE of 22.2% leaves ₹38.7 Cr of short-term borrowings out of capital employed; on Ken Research's definition it is about 14.5% [1][35]. At the margin it is weaker: from FY24 to FY26 operating profit before interest and tax rose ₹3.8 Cr on ₹74 Cr of added capital, a pre-tax return near 5%, or about 6.5% on operating capital alone. Both are below the 8.15% to 13.5% paid on borrowings [4][1].

Related-party dealings are small: directors' pay of ₹1.08 Cr and salaries of about ₹0.25 Cr to two directors' sons [1]. Contingent liabilities are ₹1.20 Cr of tax and GST disputes. Outstanding bank guarantees are not quantified in the FY26 notes (letters of credit and guarantees were ₹9.34 Cr at September 2023), while ₹7.5 Cr of payables are backed by letters of credit and ₹12.65 Cr of deposits sit under lien [1][3]. The auditor, R Kejriwal & Co of Surat, gave an unmodified opinion with no key audit matters and no default or fund diversion in its CARO report, for a fee printed as ₹2 lakh [1]. Three items merit a question: a CARO 'no' on short-term funds used long-term, beside ₹9.7 Cr of long-term deposits; ratios restated for 'corrections of prior period errors' in the H1 FY27 note; and FY25 operating cash flow of -₹18.85 Cr in one filing and -₹18.32 Cr in another [1][5][26].

Other income was 11.8% of pre-tax profit in FY25 and 11.0% in FY26, made up in FY26 of interest ₹0.42 Cr, rebate and settlement ₹0.55 Cr and capital gains ₹0.57 Cr [1]. In H1 FY27 it was 22.6% of pre-tax profit and was not itemised [5]. The effective tax rate has run at about 25% to 26% [1][5]. Promoters held 72.13% through September 2025 and 72.61% in September 2026; an institution appears at 1.17% [6]. IPO money matched its objects: of ₹29.70 Cr, ₹20.45 Cr went to working capital, ₹6.55 Cr to general purposes and ₹2.70 Cr to costs, with no deviation [1][26][11]. But working capital absorbed ₹28.0 Cr in FY25 and ₹30.0 Cr in FY26, so the ₹20.45 Cr covered less than a year of need.

H1 FY27 is the first test of a turn. Consolidated operating cash flow was +₹0.81 Cr on profit of ₹6.6 Cr. Inventory released ₹6.2 Cr, but receivables net of unbilled conversion rose ₹10.3 Cr and payables fell ₹3.5 Cr. Free cash flow was still -₹0.9 Cr before ₹2.3 Cr of interest, and borrowings rose to ₹46.0 Cr with ₹5.0 Cr of new long-term debt [5]. The balance sheet tells the same story: trade receivables rose from ₹39.1 Cr to ₹54.7 Cr in six months, while inventory fell from ₹57.6 Cr to ₹51.4 Cr and payables from ₹40.1 Cr to ₹36.6 Cr. Equity reached ₹76.8 Cr and cash ₹4.8 Cr [5]. Break-even after two years of burn is better, not a cure.

Accounting optics against cash: profit is booked as work is done, so it leads cash by the billing and retention cycle, and the contract note shows ₹58.1 Cr due from customers at March 2026 against ₹45.9 Cr a year earlier [1]. The income is supported: 92% of non-retention debtors are under six months old and bad-debt expense was ₹0.05 Cr [1]. The issue is capital need, not fabricated profit. My read is 60% to 65% structural and 35% to 40% timing. Structural, because working capital has been 39% to 54% of revenue since FY21. Timing, because ₹300 Cr of orders, the H1 inventory release and capacity from FY28 can lower the ratio. I put 55% on FY27 operating cash flow being positive, 25% on it reaching half of profit, and 55% on borrowings above ₹50 Cr at March 2027. Working capital below 55% of revenue, or cash flow above profit in a half-year, would move me.

web_blocks.caption: Aluwind Infra-Tech: profit and loss, annual and half-year columns from the price-blind feed
web_blocks.takeaway: FY25, FY26 and half-years only; the hand-built table carries FY21 to FY24.

web_blocks.html: The aggregator's profit-and-loss columns tie to the filings: sales of ₹109 Cr in FY25, ₹138 Cr in FY26 and ₹147 Cr over the last twelve months, operating margin of 11% to 12%, and net profit of ₹8 Cr, ₹10 Cr and ₹12 Cr. Interest cost rose from ₹1 Cr to ₹2 Cr and then ₹4 Cr on a trailing basis [6]. Interest is the visible price of the working capital that the cash-flow statement says the business is carrying, and it is growing faster than profit.

web_blocks.caption: Aluwind Infra-Tech: balance sheet, March 2025 to September 2026
web_blocks.takeaway: Borrowings tripled in FY26 while reserves grew by profit alone.

web_blocks.html: The balance-sheet table shows where the money went. Borrowings rose from ₹13 Cr to ₹41 Cr and then ₹46 Cr at September 2026, total assets from ₹111 Cr to ₹171 Cr, and other assets (mostly receivables, inventory and unbilled work) from ₹100 Cr to ₹146 Cr, while fixed assets stayed near ₹9 Cr to ₹12 Cr [6]. Growth has been added to working capital, not to plant, which is why the company can show profit growth with little capital spending and still absorb cash.

web_blocks.caption: Aluwind Infra-Tech: cash flow, FY25 and FY26
web_blocks.takeaway: Free cash flow is about -₹20 Cr in both years.

web_blocks.html: The cash-flow table shows operating cash flow of ₹-19 Cr and ₹-16 Cr, investing outflows of ₹-3 Cr and ₹-13 Cr, and financing inflows of ₹26 Cr in each year. Free cash flow on the aggregator's definition was about ₹-20 Cr and ₹-21 Cr, and operating cash flow was -129% and -80% of operating profit [6]. The FY26 investing outflow includes investments in deposits and similar holdings, not only plant, so capital spending on machinery (₹4.5 Cr) is a small part of the gap. Financing, first the IPO and then bank debt, paid for the working capital.

web_blocks.caption: Aluwind Infra-Tech: working-capital and return ratios
web_blocks.takeaway: Inventory days rose from 178 to 258 in a year.

web_blocks.html: The ratio table confirms the same direction with the aggregator's definitions: debtor days of 98 and 103, inventory days of 178 and 258, payable days of 150 and 180, and a cash conversion cycle that lengthened from 126 to 181 days between FY25 and FY26 [6]. These day-counts use different denominators from the annual-report ratios quoted earlier, so compare the direction rather than the exact levels. A longer cycle means each rupee of sales ties up cash for more days before it returns, and that is the mechanism behind the negative operating cash flow.

book_paragraphs: Let me be upfront about what I could not give you. A ten-year record of Aluwind does not exist in public. The company listed in April 2024, so I had to stitch the history from the March 2024 prospectus, which restates FY21 to FY23 and the first half of FY24, then the FY24, FY25 and FY26 annual reports and the half-year results up to September 2026 [3][4][1][5]. That gives us six full years and one half. It is shorter than I would like, but it covers the small-company years, the listing and two years of real growth, and that is enough to see the pattern.

Start with the part that looks wonderful. Revenue rose from ₹21.3 Cr in FY21 to ₹138.6 Cr in FY26, about 6.5 times, roughly 45% a year. Profit after tax went from ₹0.77 Cr to ₹10.45 Cr. Operating margin, before other income, climbed from 6% in FY22 to 14% in FY24 and has stayed between 11% and 14% since [3][4][1]. If you stopped reading here you would think you had found a small compounder. Per share, though, the picture is flatter. Profit rose 38.5% from FY24 to FY26, but earnings per share rose only 1.7%, because the IPO added 66 lakh shares to a base of 1.82 Cr [4][1]. The share count has been 2,48,47,420 since April 2024, and 90,000 options were granted in January 2026 [1].

Now the part that should slow you down. Look at the cash. In FY24 the business made ₹7.5 Cr of profit and had an operating cash outflow of ₹2.3 Cr. In FY25, profit was ₹8.1 Cr and operating cash flow -₹18.9 Cr. In FY26, profit was ₹10.45 Cr and operating cash flow -₹16.3 Cr. Over FY24 to FY26 the company reported ₹26.1 Cr of profit and burned ₹37.5 Cr from operations [4][1]. The prospectus told us this could happen: 'Sustained negative cash flow could impact our growth and business' [3]. It was a risk factor in March 2024. By November 2026 it is a three-year record.

Where did the money go? Picture a facade order from start to cash. Aluminium sections and glass come into the Pune shed first. The company pays suppliers, but suppliers give credit, so part of that is borrowed from them. The units are cut, coated and assembled, so the cost sits in inventory and work in progress. The company recognises revenue as the work progresses, which is the accounting rule for contracts, so profit appears before the invoice does. That is the unbilled work. When the invoice goes out, the customer withholds a slice, the retention, until the defect liability period ends. Only then does cash arrive. At March 2026 each stage was bigger than a year before. Inventory was ₹57.6 Cr, up from ₹30.5 Cr, with raw material up from ₹17.4 Cr to ₹30.6 Cr and stores and spares from ₹5.1 Cr to ₹13.8 Cr. Unbilled work was ₹32.8 Cr. Retention held by customers was ₹13.7 Cr. And customers' advances, which fund work upfront, fell from ₹9.5 Cr to ₹5.8 Cr [1]. Add unbilled work and retention and you get ₹46.4 Cr, which is 4.4 times the year's profit: income that was booked but not yet collected.

In FY26, operating profit before working capital was ₹16.9 Cr. Inventory then took ₹27.0 Cr, receivables and unbilled work took ₹16.1 Cr, and supplier credit gave back ₹14.4 Cr. After ₹3.2 Cr of tax, operating cash flow was -₹16.3 Cr. FY25 looked the same: ₹12.6 Cr before working capital, ₹28.0 Cr absorbed by it, -₹18.9 Cr in the end [1]. Notice that the receivables are not rotten. About 92% of non-retention debtors are under six months old, and bad-debt expense was ₹0.05 Cr [1]. This is a capital need, not an accounting fraud. But a capital need is still a bill, and someone has to pay it.

Who paid? In FY25 it was the IPO. The company raised ₹27.0 Cr net in April 2024, ₹29.70 Cr gross. In FY26 it was the banks. Borrowings went from ₹13.1 Cr to ₹41.3 Cr over the year and to ₹46.0 Cr by September 2026 [1][5]. Over FY25 and FY26 the company took in ₹52.5 Cr of financing. Operations ate ₹35.2 Cr. Investing took ₹16.1 Cr, of which ₹6.0 Cr was machines and ₹12.1 Cr went into deposits under bank lien, gold and property [1]. The lines are not cheap: cash credit from ICICI and Kotak at 8.15%, a ₹10 Cr working-capital loan, and ₹9.1 Cr of unsecured bank and NBFC loans at 8.15% to 13.5% that can be called on demand, with four family members as personal guarantors [1]. Interest went from ₹1.20 Cr in FY25 to ₹2.16 Cr in FY26, and ₹2.25 Cr in H1 FY27 alone. Operating profit covered the interest 9.1 times in FY25, 6.8 times in FY26 and 4.0 times in H1 FY27, by my arithmetic.

What does that do to returns? Return on equity slipped from 19.3% to 16.1%. Break it into three pieces: margin on sales, how hard the assets work, and how much borrowed money sits on top. In FY25 that was 7.44% × 1.28 × 2.03. In FY26 it was 7.54% × 1.02 × 2.09. The margin did not move. The assets worked less hard, because they grew faster than revenue, which is the working capital again. Leverage looks flat only because IPO equity was there to dilute the new debt. The company reports a return on capital of 22.2%, but it leaves ₹38.7 Cr of short-term borrowings out of capital employed. On the definition Ken Research uses for peers, I get about 14.5% [1][35]. At the margin it is thinner. From FY24 to FY26, operating profit before interest and tax rose ₹3.8 Cr, while capital rose ₹74 Cr. That is a pre-tax return near 5%, or about 6.5% on operating capital alone, below the 8.15% to 13.5% the company pays its lenders [4][1].

Let me clear the other forensic items quickly. Related-party dealings are tiny: directors' pay of ₹1.08 Cr, two directors' sons earning ₹0.11 Cr and ₹0.13 Cr, a promoter loan repaid, and ₹0.06 Cr to the subsidiary's managing director [1]. Contingent liabilities are ₹1.20 Cr of tax and GST disputes. The FY26 notes do not quantify outstanding bank guarantees; at September 2023 guarantees and letters of credit were ₹9.34 Cr, and today ₹7.5 Cr of payables are backed by letters of credit and ₹12.65 Cr of deposits sit under lien [1][3]. The auditor, R Kejriwal & Co of Surat, gave an unmodified opinion, no key audit matters, no default and no diversion of IPO money, for a fee printed as ₹2 lakh [1]. I would still ask three questions: how the auditor's 'no' on short-term funds financing long-term uses sits beside ₹9.7 Cr of long-term deposits; what the 'corrections of prior period errors' in the H1 FY27 note were; and why FY25 operating cash flow appears as -₹18.85 Cr in one filing and -₹18.32 Cr in another [1][5][26].

Other income was 11.8% of pre-tax profit in FY25 and 11.0% in FY26. In FY26 it was interest of ₹0.42 Cr, rebate and settlement of ₹0.55 Cr and capital gains of ₹0.57 Cr. In H1 FY27 it was 22.6% of pre-tax profit and the filing does not itemise it [1][5]. Tax has run at about 25% to 26%. Promoters held 72.13% through September 2025, 72.15% in March 2026 and 72.61% in September 2026, and a domestic institution appears at 1.17% [6]. The IPO money did what it promised: ₹20.45 Cr to working capital, ₹6.55 Cr to general purposes, ₹2.70 Cr to issue costs, all used by September 2025 with no deviation [1][26][11]. Yet working capital absorbed ₹28.0 Cr in FY25 and ₹30.0 Cr in FY26, so the proceeds covered less than a year of the need.

So what changed in the latest half-year? Operating cash flow was +₹0.81 Cr on profit of ₹6.6 Cr. Inventory released ₹6.2 Cr. But receivables, net of unbilled work being invoiced, rose ₹10.3 Cr, and suppliers were paid down by ₹3.5 Cr. Free cash flow was still -₹0.9 Cr before ₹2.3 Cr of interest, and borrowings rose to ₹46.0 Cr [5]. Look at the balance sheet too. Trade receivables went from ₹39.1 Cr to ₹54.7 Cr in six months, while inventory fell from ₹57.6 Cr to ₹51.4 Cr and payables from ₹40.1 Cr to ₹36.6 Cr. Equity reached ₹76.8 Cr and cash ₹4.8 Cr. In plain words, the shed is emptying a little, the customers are paying more slowly, and the company is paying its own suppliers faster. After two years of burning cash, break-even is a better sign. It is not yet a cure.

Now the judgment you asked me to make. Is the gap timing or structural? I say 60% to 65% structural and 35% to 40% timing. It is structural because working capital has been 39% to 54% of revenue since FY21, so this has always been a capital-hungry trade, and larger facade orders may carry more unbilled work, though the mix is not disclosed. It is timing because ₹300 Cr of orders, the H1 inventory release and new capacity from FY28 can all pull the ratio down. In numbers: I give 55% to FY27 operating cash flow being positive, 25% to it reaching half of profit, and 55% to borrowings above ₹50 Cr at March 2027. If net working capital falls below 55% of revenue, or cash flow beats profit in a half-year, I will move my view, and I will tell you.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Profit that has not turned into cash is a loan you have made to your customers. For two years Aluwind's shareholders and banks have made that loan on its behalf: ₹26.1 Cr of profit, ₹37.5 Cr of cash burned, debt tripled. The receivables are good, and the audit is clean. The test now is simple: show cash above profit in a single half-year, and the story changes.
